question: As a result of too many inappropriate EU standards and the Commission’s blindness to the harmful consequences of its free-trade dogma, a large proportion of our farmers are plunging into crisis. The Commission must now acknowledge their plight and urgently adopt strong measures to loosen the regulatory red tape that is choking our producers. 1.

At a time when the decline in cattle numbers is accelerating throughout Europe, does the Commission intend to relax the ban on turning over permanent grassland, which no longer reflects the reality of livestock farming?

A derogation from the obligation imposed under GAEC 8 to keep 4 % of land fallow has been granted for 2023 and 2024, to ensure that all available arable land is put to good use and that our food security is not compromised. Does the Commission intend to extend this derogation until 2027?

The trilogue on the revision of the directive on industrial emissions agreed to reduce the thresholds, bringing small-scale, family-run poultry and pig farms within its scope. Is the Commission aware of the major financial and administrative threat that this reduction poses for the industries concerned?
answer: The Commission is aware of structural changes in certain Member States leading to a reduction of the livestock herds and conversion of some farms towards arable crops.

Reacting to this situation, the Commission is discussing with Member States how the rules on the implementation of good agricultural and environmental condition standard 1 (GAEC 1) (1), concerning maintenance of the permanent grassland ratio may be adapted in light of those changes. The partial derogation to GAEC 8 (2) was granted for 2024 in the light of exceptional circumstances.

Improving biodiversity on farms has benefits for agricultural profitability and is needed to maintain the resilience of ecosystem services in the long-term. Listening to the concerns voiced by farmers in protests across the EU, fair income is a key concern.

The Commission will continue to reflect how to address the farmers’ economic concerns while ensuring that the path of green transition benefits to farming, brings new financing opportunities and guarantees food security for 2025 and onwards (3).

Lastly, the provisional political agreement reached by the European Parliament and Council on the revision of the Industrial Emissions Directive (IED) (4) does not include small-scale livestock farming. The revised IED allows Member States to register livestock farms instead of issuing a permit for each farm, as under the current IED. This will decrease administrative burden.

Livestock farms will operate according to common EU environmental standards, to be developed in cooperation with the pig and poultry sector. This will ensure the proportionality and economic viability of the IED requirements, based on the best viable techniques already used by farmers. Moreover, farmers will have a long time to adapt, as the requirements will become applicable in the course of 2030 — 2032.
